title: Basil Pesto
description: Vivid green and intensely fragrant, with toasted pine nuts, parmesan and just a whisper of garlic. Made in short pulses so the basil stays bright and the texture stays coarse.

steps.text: Toast the pine nuts in a small dry frying pan over a medium-low heat, shaking often, until pale gold. Tip onto a plate straight away and leave to cool completely.
steps.tip: Do not walk away. Pine nuts go from golden to burnt in seconds, and they carry on colouring if left in the hot pan.

steps.text: Put the cooled pine nuts, garlic and salt in a food processor and pulse to a coarse crumb.
Add the basil and pulse in short bursts, scraping down the sides once or twice, until finely chopped but not puréed.
steps.tip: Short pulses matter. Running the motor continuously heats the leaves, which turns the pesto dark and slightly bitter.

steps.text: Add the parmesan and pulse briefly to combine. Scrape into a bowl and stir in the olive oil by hand until you have a loose, spoonable sauce. Taste and add more salt if needed.

To use with pasta, take the drained pasta off the heat and toss it with the pesto and a few tablespoons of the starchy cooking water until it coats glossily. This quantity dresses about 400 g of dried pasta.

tips: Never cook pesto. Direct heat dulls the basil and makes the cheese clump, so always combine it with pasta off the heat.
With a pestle and mortar, pound the garlic and salt first, then the pine nuts, then the basil a handful at a time, and finally work in the cheese and oil. It takes longer but gives a creamier result.

substitutions.note: toast them in the same way
or half and half; pecorino is saltier, so hold back on the salt

storage: Spoon into a small jar, level the top and cover with a thin layer of olive oil. Keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days, or freeze in an ice-cube tray for up to 3 months.
author: Simmer
